**(Surah Quraysh)**
It has four verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh, their accustomed security in the caravan of winter and summer.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh, their accustomed security.﴾

Know that there are several issues here.

**Issue one:** The *lām* (the particle "li-") in His saying "*li-ilāfi*" (لِإيلافِ, "for the accustomed security of") admits of three possibilities. It is either connected to the surah before it, or to the verse after it, or connected to neither what precedes it nor what follows it.

As for the first possibility, namely that it is connected to what precedes it, there are several interpretations.

The first, which is the view of al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj) and Abu 'Ubayda, is that the implied sense is: ﴿and He made them like stalks eaten up﴾ *for the sake of the Quraysh's accustomed security*. That is, God destroyed the companions of the Elephant so that the Quraysh would remain, and so that they would keep the accustomed caravans of winter and summer. If it is said: this is weak, because they were made ﴿like stalks eaten up﴾ on account of their disbelief, and they were not made so for the sake of the Quraysh's accustomed security.

We say: this objection is weak for several reasons.

The first: We do not concede that God did this to them because of their disbelief. The recompense for disbelief is deferred until the Resurrection. God the Exalted said: ﴿This Day every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17], and He said: ﴿Had God taken people to task for what they earned, He would not have left upon it [the earth] a single creature﴾ [Fatir: 45]. Moreover, if He had done this to them because of their disbelief, He would have done it to all the disbelievers. Rather, He did this to them only: ﴿for the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾, and to magnify their rank and display their status.

The second: Grant that deterring them from disbelief was intended. It does not preclude that something else was also intended, so that the ruling is established by the two matters together.

The third: Grant that they were destroyed for their disbelief alone. Still, since that destruction led to the Quraysh's accustomed security, it is permissible to say: "They were destroyed for the accustomed security of the Quraysh," as in His saying: ﴿that it might be to them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. They did not pick him up for that purpose, but when the matter came to that outcome it was fitting that the picking up should pave the way for it.

[p. 98]

The second interpretation: the implied sense is: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the Elephant *for the accustomed security of the Quraysh*?" It is as if He, the Exalted, said: Everything We did to them, We did it for the accustomed security of the Quraysh. For He, the Exalted, made their scheme go astray, and sent against them birds in flocks, until they became like stalks eaten up. All of that happened only for the sake of the Quraysh's accustomed security.

The third interpretation: the *lām* in His saying "*li-ilāfi*" is in the sense of *ilā* ("to"). It is as if He said: We did all that We did in the preceding surah *as a further blessing upon them*, namely their accustomed security in the caravan of winter and summer. You say: "God's blessing is a blessing, and a blessing upon a blessing is the same in meaning." This is the view of al-Farra'. These are three possibilities based on connecting the *lām* to the surah before this one.

Two further points remain from the discussion of this view.

The first: People differ on connecting this *lām* to the preceding surah, and there are two views.

One of them: They made the two surahs one surah, and argued for it with several points.

The first: Each of the two surahs must be independent in itself, and since the opening of this surah is connected to the preceding surah, it must not be an independent surah.

The second: Ubayy ibn Ka'b placed them in his codex as one surah.

The third: It is reported that 'Umar recited in the Maghrib prayer, in the first rak'a, *al-Tīn*, and in the second *Alam tara* and *li-ilāfi Quraysh* together, without separating them by *bismillāh al-Rahmān al-Rahīm*.

The second view, which is the well-known and widely transmitted one, is that this surah is separate from the Surah of the Elephant. As for the connection of the beginning of this surah to what precedes it, it is not a proof for what they have said, because the whole Qur'an is like one surah and like one verse: some of it confirms other parts and some of it clarifies the meaning of others. Do you not see that the verses that indicate threat are unrestricted, yet they are connected, according to those who hold this, to the verses of repentance and the verses of pardon? And His saying ﴿We sent it down﴾ [al-Qadr: 1] is connected to what precedes it, the mention of the Qur'an. As for his saying that Ubayy did not separate them, this is opposed by the consensus of all on separating them. As for the recitation of 'Umar, it does not indicate that they are one surah, because the imam may recite two surahs.

**The second issue,** concerning this view: an explanation of why what God did to the companions of the Elephant became a cause for the accustomed security of the Quraysh. We say: there is no doubt that Mecca was empty of crops and livestock, as God the Exalted said: ﴿in a valley without cultivation﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], up to His saying: ﴿so make hearts among people incline toward them and provide them with fruits﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. The nobles of Mecca used to travel for trade on these two journeys, and they would bring for themselves and for the people of their town what they needed of food and clothing. They would profit on their journeys. Moreover, the kings of the regions used to honor the people of Mecca and say: "These are the neighbors of God's House, the residents of His sanctuary, and the custodians of the Ka'ba." To the point that they used to call the people of Mecca "the people of God." So, had the Abyssinians succeeded in what they had resolved upon, namely demolishing the Ka'ba, this honor would have departed from them, and those privileges of esteem and reverence would have ended. The people of Mecca would have become like the people of the other regions, snatched away on every side, and attacked in their persons and property. When God destroyed the companions of the Elephant and turned their scheme back against them, the people of Mecca's standing in hearts increased, and the kings of the outlying lands increased their honor of them. Those benefits and commercial gains therefore increased. For this reason God the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the Elephant?﴾ [al-Fil: 1] ﴿For the accustomed security of the Quraysh﴾ . . . ﴿in the caravan of winter and summer﴾.

The second point, which indicates the soundness of this view: His saying, the Exalted, at the end of this surah: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House, who﴾ is an allusion to the beginning of the Surah of the Elephant. It is as if He said:

[p. 99]

"So let them worship the Lord of this House, which the companions of the Elephant intended. Then the Lord of the House repelled them from their aim for the sake of your accustomed security and your benefit, because the command to worship is only fitting when it is conditioned on conveying a benefit." This indicates that the beginning of this surah is connected to the preceding surah.

The second view: the *lām* in "*li-ilāfi*" is connected to His saying "*fa-l-ya'budū*" ("so let them worship"). This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and the implied sense is: "So let them worship the Lord of this House, *for the accustomed security of the Quraysh*." That is, let them make their worship a thanks for this blessing and an acknowledgment of it. If it is said: Why did the *fā'* (the "fa-") enter in His saying "*fa-l-ya'budū*"? We say: Because the sentence contains the sense of a condition. The blessings of God upon them are countless, so it is as if it were said: "If they do not worship Him for all His other blessings, then let them worship Him for this one, which is a manifest blessing."

The third view: this *lām* is connected to neither what precedes it nor what follows it. Al-Zajjaj said: Some people said: this *lām* is the *lām* of wonder, as if the meaning were: "Wonder at the accustomed security of the Quraysh!" This is because every day they grow in misguidance, ignorance, and immersion in the worship of idols, while God gathers their scattered affairs, wards off calamities from them, and orders the means of their livelihood. There is no doubt that this is in the utmost degree of wonder at the great forbearance and generosity of God. Its parallel in the language is your saying: "For Zayd, and what we did with him!" and "For Zayd, and our honoring him!" This is the choice of al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, and al-Farra'.

\* \* \*

**The second issue:** They mentioned three aspects for *al-ilāf* (الإيلاف, "accustomed security").

The first: *al-ilāf* is *al-ilf* (الإلف, "familiarity, habitual attachment"). The scholars of language said: *alifa al-shay'* and *alafahu* (ألِفْتُ الشَّيْءَ وألَفْتُهُ), *ilfan*, *ilāfan*, and *īlāfan* have one meaning: I kept to it, adhered to it. So the meaning is: "for the familiarity of the Quraysh with these two journeys," so that they would be connected and not cut off. Abu Ja'far recited "*li-ilfi Quraysh*" (لِإلْفِ قُرَيْشٍ), and the others recited "*li-ilāfi Quraysh*" (لِإلافِ قُرَيْشٍ), and 'Ikrima recited "*li-īlāfi Quraysh*" (لِيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ).

The second: This may come from your saying: "I kept to such-and-such a place, and God made me keep to it" (*alzamanīhi Allāh*). Thus you say: "I became familiar with such-and-such" (*alifa kadhā*), and "God made me familiar with it" (*alafanīhi Allāh*). The meaning is the establishment of familiarity through a providence containing subtle kindness. One becomes familiar with something by oneself (*alifa binafsihi ilfan*), and another makes one familiar with it (*āla fahu ghayruhu ilāfan*). The meaning is that this familiarity came about in the Quraysh by the providence of God. This is like His saying: ﴿But God brought their hearts together﴾ [al-Anfal: 63], and He said: ﴿So He brought your hearts together, and by His blessing you became brothers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103]. Gladness may be a cause of intimacy and agreement, as occurred when the companions of the Elephant were defeated and the Quraysh rejoiced. So the verbal noun here is in the genitive construction with the object, and the meaning is: "in order that God might make the Quraysh constant in their two journeys."

The third: *al-ilāf* may be preparation and equipping (*al-tahyi'a wal-tajhīz*). This is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi. On this view the verbal noun is in the genitive construction with the subject, and the meaning is: "for the Quraysh's equipping of their two journeys, so that they would be connected and not cut off." Abu Ja'far recited "*li-līfi*" (لِيلافِ) without a hamza, deleting the hamza of the *if'āl* form entirely. This is in accordance with his school in "*yastahzi'ūna*" (يَسْتَهْزِءُونَ), and its explanation has already passed.

**The third issue:** The repetition in His saying "*li-ilāfi Quraysh*" ... "*ilāfihim*" is that He first stated the *ilāf* in an unrestricted form, then made the restricted form a substitute for that unrestricted one, to magnify the matter of the *ilāf* and to remind of the great favor in it. The closer view is that His saying "*li-ilāfi Quraysh*" is general, encompassing every intimacy and agreement they had, so it includes their standing, their conduct, and all their circumstances. Then He specified the accustomed security of the two journeys for mention, because it is the mainstay of their livelihood, as in His saying: ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqara: 98]. The benefit of omitting the conjunctive *wāw* is to draw attention to the fact that this is the whole of the blessing. The Arabs say: "*aliftu kadhā*" (ألِفْتُ كَذا), meaning "I kept to it." Obligation (*al-ilzām*) is of two kinds: obligation through commandment and duty, and obligation through affection and intimacy. For when a person loves something, he keeps to it. From this is His saying: ﴿and He made them keep to the word of piety﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. Likewise compulsion (*al-ilja'*) is of two kinds:

The first: to repel harm, like fleeing from a beast of prey.

The second: to seek a great benefit, like someone who finds great wealth, with no obstacle to taking it, whether rational, legal, or sensory. He is as one compelled to take it. Similarly, the motives that fall short of compulsion: sometimes they are to repel harm and sometimes to attract benefit. [p. 100] This latter is what is meant in His saying: "*ilāfihim*" (إيلافِهِمْ, "their accustomed security").

**The fourth issue:** They agreed that the Quraysh are the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinana. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "We are the sons of al-Nadr ibn Kinana; we do not claim a mother other than our mother, nor do we disown our father." They have mentioned several reasons for this naming:

The first: It is the diminutive of *al-qirsh* (القِرْش), a great creature in the sea that harasses ships and does not move except by fire. It is reported from Mu'awiya that he asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Why were the Quraysh named?" He said: "After a creature in the sea that eats and is not eaten, that rises and is not risen above," and he recited:

*And the Quraysh are those who dwell in the sea:*
*by them the Quraysh was named Quraysh.*

The diminutive is for magnification. It is known that the Quraysh are described by these attributes, because they hold charge of the community, for the imams are from the Quraysh.

The second: It is derived from *al-qirsh*, which means earning, because they were earners through their trade and their travels in the lands.

The third: al-Layth said: They were scattered outside the sanctuary, so Qusayy ibn Kilab gathered them within the sanctuary until they made it their dwelling. So they named them Quraysh, because *al-taqarrush* is gathering. It is said: "The people *taqarrashū*" when they assembled. For this reason Qusayy was called "the Gatherer" (*mujammi'*). The poet said:

*Your father Qusayy used to be called "the Gatherer,"*
*by him God gathered the tribes from Fihr.*

The fourth: They used to fill the need of the poor pilgrims, and so they were named Quraysh, because *al-qirsh* means searching. Ibn Hurra said:

*O you who gloats and searches out our affairs before 'Amr,*
*and is there any lasting for that?*

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the journeys of winter and summer﴾: concerning this there are issues.

The first issue: al-Layth said: al-Rihlah (the journey) is the noun for departing from a people to set out, and regarding the meaning of this rihlah there are two views.

The first, which is the well-known one: the commentators said that Quraysh had two journeys, a journey in winter to Yemen, because Yemen is warmer, and a journey in summer to al-Sham. ʿAṭāʾ reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the reason for this was that when one of them was struck by famine (makhmasah), he would go out with his dependants to a place and they would pitch a tent over themselves until they died. Then Hashim ibn ʿAbd Manaf came, and he was the chief of his people. He had a son called Asad, and Asad had a companion (tirb) from the Banu Makhzum whom he loved and played with. [This companion] complained to him of the harm and hunger, so Asad went in to his mother weeping. She sent to those [people] with flour and fat, and they lived on it for some days. Then Asad's companion came to him again a second time and complained to him of hunger. Hashim stood up as an orator among Quraysh and said: "You have been struck by a barren year (jadb) in which you are reduced in number and humiliated, and you are the people of God's Sanctuary and the nobles of the children of Adam, and the people are followers of you." They said: "We are followers of yours, so there is no opposition from us against you." So he gathered every clan of one father for the two journeys, in winter to Yemen and in summer to al-Sham, for trade. Whatever the rich man gained, he divided between himself and the poor man, until their poor became like their rich. Then Islam came while they were still upon this. No tribe of the Arabs had more wealth or greater honour than Quraysh. A poet said about them:

The ones who mix their poor with their rich,
until their poor becomes like one who is sufficient.

Know that the aspect of the blessing and favour in this is that if what the People of the Elephant intended had been achieved, the people of the regions would have ceased to honour them. Also, they would have scattered, and their condition would have become like the condition of the Jews mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We divided them in the earth into nations﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 168].

Page 101

The gathering of one tribe in one place is more included in the blessing than that the gathering should be from various tribes. He, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that among the conditions of travel is companionship and familiarity, and from this is His saying: ﴿nor is there disputing in the pilgrimage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. Travel is more in need of noble character than residence.

The second view: the intended meaning is the journey of the people to the people of Makkah. The journey of winter and summer is the ʿUmrah of Rajab and the Ḥajj of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, because one of them was in winter and the other in summer, and the season of Makkah's benefits occurs through these two. If what the People of the Elephant intended had been achieved, this benefit would have been stopped.

The second issue: the accusative of rihlah is with ʾīlāfihim as its object (mafʿūl bihi), and he intended the two journeys of winter and summer, so he used the singular for the sake of avoiding confusion, like His saying: "Eat in part of your belly." It was also said: its meaning is the journey of winter and the journey of summer. It was read as "Riḥlatu" with a ḍammah on the rāʾ, and it means the direction (al-jihah).

The meaning is that this familiarity came about in the Quraysh by the providence of God. This is like His saying: ﴿But God brought their hearts together﴾ [al-Anfal: 63], and He said: ﴿So He brought your hearts together, and by His blessing you became brothers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103]. Gladness may be a cause of intimacy and agreement, as occurred when the companions of the Elephant were defeated and the Quraysh rejoiced. So the verbal noun here is in the genitive construction with the object, and the meaning is: "in order that God might make the Quraysh constant in their two journeys."

The third: *al-ilāf* may be preparation and equipping (*al-tahyi'a wal-tajhīz*). This is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi. On this view the verbal noun is in the genitive construction with the subject, and the meaning is: "for the Quraysh's equipping of their two journeys, so that they would be connected and not cut off." Abu Ja'far recited "*li-līfi*" (لِيلافِ) without a hamza, deleting the hamza of the *if'āl* form entirely. This is in accordance with his school in "*yastahzi'ūna*" (يَسْتَهْزِءُونَ), and its explanation has already passed.

**The third issue:** The repetition in His saying "*li-ilāfi Quraysh*" ... "*ilāfihim*" is that He first stated the *ilāf* in an unrestricted form, then made the restricted form a substitute for that unrestricted one, to magnify the matter of the *ilāf* and to remind of the great favor in it. The closer view is that His saying "*li-ilāfi Quraysh*" is general, encompassing every intimacy and agreement they had, so it includes their standing, their conduct, and all their circumstances. Then He specified the accustomed security of the two journeys for mention, because it is the mainstay of their livelihood, as in His saying: ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqara: 98]. The benefit of omitting the conjunctive *wāw* is to draw attention to the fact that this is the whole of the blessing. The Arabs say: "*aliftu kadhā*" (ألِفْتُ كَذا), meaning "I kept to it." Obligation (*al-ilzām*) is of two kinds: obligation through commandment and duty, and obligation through affection and intimacy. For when a person loves something, he keeps to it. From this is His saying: ﴿and He made them keep to the word of piety﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. Likewise compulsion (*al-ilja'*) is of two kinds:

The first: to repel harm, like fleeing from a beast of prey.

The second: to seek a great benefit, like someone who finds great wealth, with no obstacle to taking it, whether rational, legal, or sensory. He is as one compelled to take it. Similarly, the motives that fall short of compulsion: sometimes they are to repel harm and sometimes to attract benefit. [p. 100] This latter is what is meant in His saying: "*ilāfihim*" (إيلافِهِمْ, "their accustomed security").

**The fourth issue:** They agreed that the Quraysh are the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinana. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "We are the sons of al-Nadr ibn Kinana; we do not claim a mother other than our mother, nor do we disown our father." They have mentioned several reasons for this naming:

The first: It is the diminutive of *al-qirsh* (القِرْش), a great creature in the sea that harasses ships and does not move except by fire. It is reported from Mu'awiya that he asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Why were the Quraysh named?" He said: "After a creature in the sea that eats and is not eaten, that rises and is not risen above," and he recited:

*And the Quraysh are those who dwell in the sea:*
*by them the Quraysh was named Quraysh.*

The diminutive is for magnification. It is known that the Quraysh are described by these attributes, because they hold charge of the community, for the imams are from the Quraysh.

The second: It is derived from *al-qirsh*, which means earning, because they were earners through their trade and their travels in the lands.

The third: al-Layth said: They were scattered outside the sanctuary, so Qusayy ibn Kilab gathered them within the sanctuary until they made it their dwelling. So they named them Quraysh, because *al-taqarrush* is gathering. It is said: "The people *taqarrashū*" when they assembled. For this reason Qusayy was called "the Gatherer" (*mujammi'*). The poet said:

*Your father Qusayy used to be called "the Gatherer,"*
*by him God gathered the tribes from Fihr.*

The fourth: They used to fill the need of the poor pilgrims, and so they were named Quraysh, because *al-qirsh* means searching. Ibn Hurra said:

*O you who gloats and searches out our affairs before 'Amr,*
*and is there any lasting for that?*

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the journeys of winter and summer﴾: concerning this there are issues.

The first issue: al-Layth said: al-Rihlah (the journey) is the noun for departing from a people to set out, and regarding the meaning of this rihlah there are two views.

The first, which is the well-known one: the commentators said that Quraysh had two journeys, a journey in winter to Yemen, because Yemen is warmer, and a journey in summer to al-Sham. ʿAṭāʾ reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the reason for this was that when one of them was struck by famine (makhmasah), he would go out with his dependants to a place and they would pitch a tent over themselves until they died. Then Hashim ibn ʿAbd Manaf came, and he was the chief of his people. He had a son called Asad, and Asad had a companion (tirb) from the Banu Makhzum whom he loved and played with. [This companion] complained to him of the harm and hunger, so Asad went in to his mother weeping. She sent to those [people] with flour and fat, and they lived on it for some days. Then Asad's companion came to him again a second time and complained to him of hunger. Hashim stood up as an orator among Quraysh and said: "You have been struck by a barren year (jadb) in which you are reduced in number and humiliated, and you are the people of God's Sanctuary and the nobles of the children of Adam, and the people are followers of you." They said: "We are followers of yours, so there is no opposition from us against you." So he gathered every clan of one father for the two journeys, in winter to Yemen and in summer to al-Sham, for trade. Whatever the rich man gained, he divided between himself and the poor man, until their poor became like their rich. Then Islam came while they were still upon this. No tribe of the Arabs had more wealth or greater honour than Quraysh. A poet said about them:

The ones who mix their poor with their rich,
until their poor becomes like one who is sufficient.

Know that the aspect of the blessing and favour in this is that if what the People of the Elephant intended had been achieved, the people of the regions would have ceased to honour them. Also, they would have scattered, and their condition would have become like the condition of the Jews mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We divided them in the earth into nations﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 168].

Page 101

The gathering of one tribe in one place is more included in the blessing than that the gathering should be from various tribes. He, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that among the conditions of travel is companionship and familiarity, and from this is His saying: ﴿nor is there disputing in the pilgrimage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. Travel is more in need of noble character than residence.

The second view: the intended meaning is the journey of the people to the people of Makkah. The journey of winter and summer is the ʿUmrah of Rajab and the Ḥajj of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, because one of them was in winter and the other in summer, and the season of Makkah's benefits occurs through these two. If what the People of the Elephant intended had been achieved, this benefit would have been stopped.

The second issue: the accusative of rihlah is with ʾīlāfihim as its object (mafʿūl bihi), and he intended the two journeys of winter and summer, so he used the singular for the sake of avoiding confusion, like His saying: "Eat in part of your belly." It was also said: its meaning is the journey of winter and the journey of summer. It was read as "Riḥlatu" with a ḍammah on the rāʾ, and it means the direction (al-jihah).

**Its statement (Exalted is He): ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾.** Know that favour (*inʿam*) is of two kinds:

First: the averting of harm (*daf ʿal-darar*).

Second: the bringing of benefit (*jalb al-nafʿ*). The first is more important and comes first. For this reason they said: averting harm from oneself is obligatory, whereas bringing benefit is not obligatory. For this reason, Exalted is He, mentioned the blessing of averting harm in Surat al-Fil and the blessing of bringing benefit in this surah. Since it is established that favour must be met with thankfulness and devotion, He therefore followed the mention of the blessing with the demand for devotion, saying: (so let them worship). Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** We have mentioned that worship (*ʿibadah*) is humbling oneself and submitting to the one worshipped to the utmost degree. Then some said: He meant, "So let them affirm the oneness (*tawhid*) of the Lord of this House, because He is the One who protected the House and not the idols, and because affirming the oneness of God is the key to all acts of worship." Others said: The intended meaning is the acts of worship connected with the actions of the limbs, and then he mentioned each category of the types of worship. The better view is to take it in its entirety, because the wording encompasses all of them except what the evidence excludes. There is another interpretation of the verse, which is that the meaning of "so let them worship" is: so let them abandon the journey of winter and summer, and occupy themselves with the worship of the Lord of this House, for He feeds them from hunger and secures them from fear. Perhaps the specification of the word "Lord" confirms what they had said to Abraha: "The House has a Lord who will protect it," and they did not rely on the idols in that. Thus it became binding upon them, by their own acknowledgement, that they should not worship other than Him. It is as if He is saying: Since you relied on Me for protection, then direct your worship and service to Me.

**The second issue:** The reference to the House in this wording conveys glorification. For He, glory be to Him, sometimes attributes the servant to Himself, saying: "O My servants," and sometimes He attributes Himself to the servant, saying: "your God." Likewise, in the case of the House, (sometimes) He attributes Himself to the House, which is His saying: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾, and sometimes He attributes the House to Himself, saying: ﴿Purify My House﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125].

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who fed them against hunger﴾ And there are several aspects to this feeding:

The first: When He granted them security in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), so that they would not be attacked during their journeys, this was the cause of their being fed after the hunger they had been in.

The second: Muqatil said: It was difficult for them to travel to Yemen and Syria in winter and summer in search of provision. So God cast into the hearts of the Abyssinians that they should carry food by ships to Mecca, and they did so. The people of Mecca began going out to them with camels and wine, buying their food from Jeddah at a distance of two nights' journey, and this continued. Thus God spared them the burden of the two journeys.

The third: al-Kalbi said:

Page 102
The meaning of this verse is that when they denied Muhammad (ﷺ), he invoked against them, saying: "O God, make it upon them as years of Joseph (were years of famine)." Severe drought fell upon them and they were struck by hardship, and they said: "O Muhammad, pray to God for us, for we are believers." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed, and the lands became fertile, and the people of Mecca became prosperous after the drought." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Who fed them against hunger﴾. Then there are questions concerning the verse:

The first question: Worship is obligatory because God has given the foundations of blessings, and feeding is not among the foundations of blessings, so why did He give feeding as the reason for the obligation of worship? The answer has several aspects:

The first: When He mentioned His favour upon them by holding back the elephant, sending the birds, and destroying the Abyssinians, and explained that He did that for their Ilaf (the security of their journeys), then commanded them to worship, it is as if the questioner says: "But we need to earn food and defend ourselves, so if we occupy ourselves with worship, who will feed us?" So He said: "The One who fed them against hunger" before they worshipped Him will not feed them when they worship Him?

The second: After God had given the servant the foundations of blessings, the servant wronged Him, yet He feeds them in spite of that. It is as if God says: "If you are not ashamed before the foundations of blessings, are you not ashamed before My kindness to you after your wrongdoing?!"

The third: He mentioned feeding because a beast obeys whoever feeds it. It is as if God says: "You are not beneath the beast."

The second question: Has He not made the world a possession for us by His words: ﴿He created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]? So how is it fitting to bestow favour upon us by giving us our own possession? The answer: Consider the things that are necessary before eating, so that the food is completed and prepared, and the things that are necessary after eating, so that the benefit of the food consumed is completed. You know that the spheres and the stars are necessary, and the four elements are necessary for that food to be complete, and the whole body with its different shapes and forms is necessary so that benefit from the food is complete. Then you will know that feeding is fitting with the command to obedience and worship.

The third question: Bestowing favour through feeding is not befitting one who has any generosity, so how about the Most Generous of the generous? The answer: The purpose is not bestowing favour, but guidance to what is best, because the purpose of eating is not to strengthen desire, which prevents obedience, but to strengthen the body to perform acts of obedience. So it is as if the purpose of the command to worship is that.

The fourth question: What is the benefit of His words "against hunger"? The answer: There are benefits in it:

The first: A warning that the matter of hunger is severe, and from this is His words: ﴿And He it is who sends down rain after they had despaired﴾ [al-Shura: 28], and the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever wakes up secure in his dwelling..." the hadith.

The second: Reminding them of the former state, the bad and painful one, which is hunger, so that they recognise the value of the present blessing.

The third: A warning that the best food is that which satisfies hunger, for He did not say "and satisfied them," because food removes hunger, whereas satiation produces bloating (al-bitnah).

* As for His words: ﴿And made them secure from fear﴾, there are several interpretations of it:

The first: They used to travel secure, no one harming them, and no one raiding them, neither on their journeys nor at home, while others were not safe from raids on journeys or at home. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a safe sanctuary?﴾ [al-Ankabut: 67].

The second: He made them secure from the crowding of the People of the Elephant.

The third: al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: He made them secure from the fear of leprosy (al-judham), so it would not strike them in their land.

Page 103
Leprosy.
The fourth: He made them secure from the fear that leadership (al-khilafah) would be in others than them.

The fifth: He made them secure through Islam, for they used to reflect in disbelief and know that the religion they were upon was nothing, yet they did not know the religion that a sensible person must hold fast to.

The sixth: He fed them from the hunger of ignorance with the food of Revelation, and made them secure from the fear of misguidance by the clarification of guidance. It is as if God says: "O people of Mecca, before the mission of Muhammad you were called the ignorant of the Arabs and their boors, and those who disputed with you were called the People of the Book. Then I sent down Revelation upon your Prophet, and taught you the Book and wisdom, until you are now called the People of Knowledge and the Qur'an, while those were called the ignorant Jews and Christians. Moreover, feeding the body with food that is its nourishment obliges thanks, so feeding with the food that is nourishment of the soul should surely oblige thanks!" And there are questions concerning the verse:

The first question: Why did He not say "from hunger and from fear" (ʿan)? We say: Because the meaning of "ʿan" is that He made hunger distant from them, and this requires that such distancing be preceded by enduring hunger for a time, and then He removes it from them. But "min" does not require that; rather its meaning is that when they hunger they are fed, and whenever they fear they are made secure.

The second question: Why did He say "min hunger, min fear" in the indefinite form? The answer: The purpose of indefiniteness is magnification. As for hunger, it is because of what we have related: that a severe hardship struck them until they ate carrion and burnt bones. As for fear, it is the intense fear that came from the People of the Elephant. It may also be that the purpose of indefiniteness is belittling, the meaning being that since God, for the sake of His utmost generosity, did not permit them to remain in that slight hunger and slight fear, how could it be permissible in His generosity, if they worship Him, that He would neglect their affair?! It may also be that the meaning is: "He fed them from hunger" other than hunger, "and made them secure from fear" other than fear, so that the second hunger and the second fear would remind them of what they had been in first of kinds of hunger and fear, so that they would be thankful from one aspect and patient from another, and thus deserve the reward of both qualities.

The third question: God fed them and made them secure only in answer to the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. As for feeding, it is His words: ﴿and provide for its people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126], and as for security, it is His words: ﴿Make this city secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. If that is so, it was a favour upon Ibrahim, peace be upon him, so how did He make it a favour upon those present? The answer: When God said: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], Ibrahim said: ﴿And from my descendants﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], and God said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. So Ibrahim called upon Him with this courtesy, and when he said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126], He restricted it with His words: ﴿whoever of them believes in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126]. God said: There is no need for this restriction; rather, whoever disbelieves, I will let him enjoy a little. It is as if God said: As for the blessing of security, it is religious, so it is attained only by one who is pious; but as for the blessing of this world, it reaches the righteous and the wicked, the good and the evil. If that is so, then feeding the disbeliever against hunger and securing him from fear is a favour from God bestowed upon him from the outset, not by the supplication of Ibrahim, and the question is resolved. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best, and may God bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
